title: IMF sounds alarm on rising government borrowing costs – business live
summary:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

  • Global financial system is failing developing countries, says Ed Miliband

Wednesday morning at the IMF/World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok saw IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva give her opening press conference, our economics editor Heather Stewart writes.

She enthusiastically reiterated the IMF’s call for major economies - including the US - to implement tougher fiscal policies. “Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house, before the cracks widen,” she said - and later:

“Fundamentals matter. Get your house in order. Otherwise, your people, your businesses will pay a price.”

“Surplus countries need to increase domestic consumption. Deficit countries need to save more, cut debt, cut the deficits over time.”

“we need to recognise that it is not just a systemically important, signficant economy, but London is one of the capitals of the world for the finance community. And traditionally we have seen more attention in relative terms in the UK to what the government is doing, what is happening - a bit more sensitivity.”

“I think the UK government knows they need to stay the course: they need to reaffirm this confidence in the direction of travel.”

“We are seeing, across the eurozone, an impact in terms of yields edging upwards, even in countries that traditionally never see their yields move.”

“I think what countries should do from the macro perspective depends a lot in terms of their initial position. In general, however, the the defence spending will be persistent, so even if you accommodate it temporarily with debt, you have to be prepared at some point to recognise that that debt cannot forever finance this part.

And the second issue is that...in general, Europe has really high revenue ratios. So the space for a lot more revenues is not easy: it distorts, at the end of the day. So, the discussion about the social contract behind spending is very, very urgent.”

“Given the fact that many of these spending pressures are going to be persistent, there are going to be difficult trade-offs, and countries are going to have to assess carefully, in communication and dialogue and discussion with the public, in terms of what the priorities are, what needs to come first, and what governments need to spend on.”

title: Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?
summary:
The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him

  • Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

There is a manic quality to Donald Trump’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s midterm elections to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.

The US president offered to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider backtracking under pressure from the cow lobby. He offered to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies were not interested. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing $500 checks to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a $5,000 check if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will go nowhere.

title: Send us your questions for economist Isabella Weber on inflation and affordability
summary:
First Edition newsletter will be hosting a reader Q&A with economist Isabella Weber, a leading voice on inflation, affordability and cost of living and now’s your chance to put your questions to her

Isabella Weber is one of the most sought-after and influential economists of her generation, and has advised policymakers and governments in the US, Germany, Europe and Latin America.

She has become a leading voice on inflation, affordability and the cost of living. Her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics, looks at the relationship between economic insecurity and the rise of the far right, arguing progressive politics must respond to the rise of authoritarianism by urgently addressing the economic pressures people experience in their daily lives. For years Weber was treated as an outlier.

Weber is an associate professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and an associate in research at Harvard’s Fairbank Center, and is the author of the prize-winning How China Escaped Shock Therapy.

We’d love to hear your questions. Perhaps you would like to find out how the cost of living affects the current political landscape? What’s happening in the bond markets? Or the advice she’d give to progressive politicians, from incumbents like Burnham and Mamdani to the German parties taking on the AFD. From austerity to zero deficits, nothing is too simple or complex.
